speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. He said: Mr. Speaker, in speaking to Bill C-35,1 am pleased at the outset to thank all hon. members who participated in the debate on second reading and in the discussions of the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs. As was noted on these occasions, the provisions of the bill are important for all residents of Canada, especially for those who have earned social security credits in other countries but who are deprived of foreign benefits in the absence of international agreements. Now that a general consensus has been reached concerning these provisions, I trust that hon. members will want to give the bill speedy passage.
The constructive suggestions made by hon. members on all sides of the House in considering this bill are a matter of public record. I would therefore like to describe briefly certain of the measures which my department has taken in responding to them.

In addition to the public information campaign, to which I referred in committee, for conveying the provisions of the bill accurately to the general public, I intend to continue our efforts to inform fully all members of program developments. As a result of the arrangements for closer liaison between constituency offices and OAS regional offices which my department inaugurated last December, our regional directors report that the level of service to pensioners has improved and that GIS renewals are being handled more effectively. This is due in large part to the more prominent role being played by hon. members and their constituency offices in handling inquiries from pensioners. For its part, the department has improved its field services through the establishment of 76 itinerant offices. In combination, these measures have led to a more efficient resolution of pensioner problems and, in most cases, to same day replies.
My department intends to reinforce this link by providing program information to constituency offices, as we have done during the initial phases of this bill. I will, of course, continue to welcome the comments of hon. members on our progress in this area.
When the standing committee was examining the bill the other evening, one hon. member raised an objection to the fact that we require the pensioner to sign jointly with his spouse the application for spouse's allowance benefits. I undertook at that time to investigate whether a pensioner had ever refused to sign an application for spouse's benefits. Upon investigation we could find only one instance of a pensioner refusing to sign the spouse's application out of over 75,000 benefits being paid, and even this particular instance could well be justified since in some instances the fact that a spouse's allowance would be granted could result in lower GIS benefits for the pensioner. The dual signing requirement would therefore not appear to be a significant problem. At the same time there are good reasons for having this procedure.
The dual signatures give some assurance, first of all, that the couple are indeed married or have a common law relationship and are living together. The dual signatures also mean that we have the spouse's acceptance of the fact that his or her GIS may be varied downward in accordance with the rates payable under the spouse's allowance program. Therefore it would seem to be the best course to leave the matter the way it is.

It is also the government's intention to broaden the options feature under the GIS and spouse's allowance programs to provide compensation for reductions in Canada Pension Plan benefits and for cessation or reduction of alimony payments or of private carrier disability insurance payments.
GIS and spouse's allowance benefits are payable on a fiscal year basis and are based on income received in the previous calendar year. However, when a person suffers a loss of income due to termination or reduction of private pension benefits, GIS and spouse's allowance benefits may be recalculated on the basis of the estimated reduced income for the
March 9, 1977

current calendar year, thus allowing for an increase in these income-tested benefits.
Currently, the old age security regulations governing this issue do not include CPP/QPP survivors' and disability benefits, alimony or private disability insurance payments. My officials have recently reviewed this issue and have concluded that the option provisions currently covering annuity payments, unemployment insurance benefits plus superannuation and other private pension payments should also cover supplementary CPP/QPP benefits, alimony and private disability insurance payments.
I wish to thank the hon. member for Gatineau (Mr. Clermont) in particular for having brought the matter to the attention of the committee.
The government therefore intends to amend the old age security regulations so that the new option provisions become effective with the proclamation date of this bill. In the meantime, my officials will continue to study this matter with a view to clarifying whether other income items should be added to the list used to determine entitlement to income-tested benefits under the old age security program.

Time does not permit me to review all the helpful suggestions made and the efforts being deployed in following them up. The primary objectives of Bill C-35 are to permit international agreements, and to provide greater equity in the treatment of beneficiaries and consistency among the three tiers of the Canadian retirement income system. Therefore, in once again thanking all concerned for their contribution toward achieving these objectives-and assuring them of the continuing co-operation of my officials and myself-I would urge upon all hon. members the bill's speedy passage.

Mr. Speaker, as has been stated, we do not intend to hold up this bill unduly because the vast majority of us who have had anything to do with it through second reading stage, committee stage, and now third reading, find there are matters in it that have been outstanding for a considerable time which need a little tidying up.
I was pleased to note that the minister had reviewed the position which was brought to his attention by one of the lady members with regard to joint applications. It is interesting to note that out of 75,000 joint applications there was only one which was a problem, which really indicates that there is no problem whatsoever.
I am also appreciative of the fact that the minister indicated to us that certain exceptions will be made in the GIS. He mentioned that in a few cases it would be counted as income. I would respectfully point out to the minister that in committee he indicated some 18 different examples of income which would reduce GIS. As I understand it, he is looking into this matter very thoroughly. It seems to me that if anyone needs assistance in this country, it is certainly our senior citizens, to whom we owe a considerable debt, and I hope the minister will be active in this regard and that in the near future he will
Old Age Security
come up with further exemptions which would allow long-run financial assistance to our senior citizens.
I would like to take a little bit of time to review this legislation. Changes in the residency requirement respecting old age security so that the pension is earned by residents at the rate of one-fortieth of the eventual full pension for each one year of residence in Canada after age 18 mean that in order to receive the full pension one must be legally resident in Canada for 40 years. Any length of residence less than 40 years would qualify a person for an OAS pension which is a portion of the full pension calculated at the rate of one-fortieth for each year. The present residency rules create a situation whereby one either qualifies for pension or does not receive one at all. This is certainly a hardship. We have now done away with the all or nothing at all provision with respect to OAS. I must say that that is a commendable step, and it will certainly assist many people.
I think this bill is very important, and it will seem even more important when I indicate what can happen to some people who are being shortchanged. On the international level, to protect the acquired social security credits of our residents who migrate across international borders during their active years, as a result of this bill we can negotiate reciprocal agreements with other countries similar to those already in existence. This would facilitate the receipt of pension credits accumulated by immigrants in their country of origin though they now reside in Canada. Reciprocal agreements make social security portable between contracting countries and allow for the co-ordination of their social security programs.
As I understand it, we do not need this bill to start negotiating with countries such as Italy, France, the United Kingdom, Bermuda, Jamaica, etc., but it is the expressed intention of the minister to start, if not continue, discussions with the various countries so that we can be in a position to execute the documents as soon as this bill is proclaimed. As I understand it, the bill will be proclaimed as soon as possible, but the earliest date the minister can see right now is July 1.
I hope that on further reflection the minister will be able to settle on an earlier date because I do not know why, if this bill is passed tonight or perhaps tomorrow, it cannot be implemented a little earlier. In any event, we at least know he has a target date of July 1.
I would like to put on the record what this new residency requirement actually does. There has been a lot of misunderstanding. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) asked me-and I was very honoured-to second his motion regarding the press, on February 10. Not having read the bill to know what it is all about, the press, unwittingly perhaps, projected a feeling by way of reports which left people confused with respect to what is really required. 1 would like to put the following on the record:
Q. To whom would the new residence rules apply?
A. After a transition period of 40 years, to everybody. During the transition period, however, only to residents of Canada under the age of 25 when the new

Old Age Security
rules come into force, and to anyone, irrespective of age, who is not now residing in Canada or who has not had prior legal residence here after the age of 18.
That is an important statement. It indicates that the new rules apply during the transition period only to residents of Canada under the age of 25, and those coming into Canada. That is one point.
There is another point. This does get a little fuzzy unless one is extremely careful, and I want to follow it up. Regarding to whom the new residence rules apply, persons 25 or over residing in Canada or having had prior legal residence here after the age of 18 will have the opportunity, as they have now, to qualify for a full pension under the existing residence requirements. That means the present law. If they cannot qualify for a full pension under the existing rules, they could receive a partial pension related to their years of residence in Canada, under the new rules. That means that these people will have a choice, and this is where we have to be extremely careful. This is why I pointed out to the minister that we must advertise in order to bring about full awareness of the implications of the matter I just spoke of because, if one is not careful, one can be shortchanged. If people do not know what this bill is all about, they may take an early pension and get less than the amount to which they would really be entitled had they known the implications of applying for an earlier pension.
I know the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre likes to have credit given to him when it is due. He brought home very forcibly a problem which can arise. I would like to read from the committee report of February 22 wherein the hon. member was concerned about a person who would be entitled to twenty-nine fortieths of a pension because that person had that amount of time, but if he waited a further month he could have been entitled to thirty fortieths, if I can put it that way. This means that that has to be properly advertised.
By asking for an early pension a person can shortchange himself for the sake of one month. At page 19:15 the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is reported to have said the following:
Let me give you this example. I have picked figures that build up my case, but it is a case that could take place. Somebody is in Canada now who is over 25, which puts him in the category of having the choice. He stays here until he is 43-that is 18 years-and then he goes away. He comes back at age 62. So, at age 65 he has had 18 years that he was here earlier and three more, which makes 21. So, under the new rule he qualifies for 21/40ths of the pension.

But let us take that same person who had 18 years here before. Under the old rule, on the three for one basis, that is worth six years. He has now been here from age 62 to 65, three years, that is nine years. If he waited one more year, instead of getting 21 /40ths of the pension he would get 100 per cent under the old rule. I do not think it is good enough just to spell out the rules. I think the person who comes along with that record should be told, 'Look, brother, one more year and you will get 100 per cent instead of 21/40ths.'
That is what I mean by a shortchange provision. We are very happy to have had the wisdom and expertise of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, who zeroed in on this, but what do we intend to do? Well, the minister says he realizes that if people are not careful they will be shortchanged, and once they are shortchanged there will be no

turning back. We cannot turn back the clock, although the minister said that perhaps there would be some consideration given. However, the way the act is drafted, once a person applies and his application is approved, he has had it. In that way people can be shortchanged.
I am pleased that the minister mentioned the new liaison he has with the regional offices which are dealing with local constituencies in order to help senior citizens understand not only OAS but everything else which has to be done in terms of completing forms. We are concerned about whether there will be proper counselling. They should be told, "Under the regulations, if you take this pension now you are going to be shortchanged, so wait a month or two years, depending upon the circumstances, and you will be able to take full advantage of the act."
What 1 asked for, what I think the minister will do, and what should be done, is the provision of counselling services immediately the act is proclaimed so that no one will be shortchanged. In other words, I do not want the onus to be on the applicant; I want the onus to be on the government to protect our senior citizens. The minister says he understands that, and will move in that direction, not only on the domestic level but internationally as well. It is extremely important that people involved in this type of program not be shortchanged. I know the minister has been said to be a hard nut at times, but in connection with our senior citizens he seems to have some sympathy-except in one area, the spouse's allowance.

Let me bring up another matter which was mentioned in committee. I am not going to be partisan because it is not a partisan matter. The government talks about restraint but it has spent $1 million trying to defend the indefensible-wage and price controls. I asked the minister, and he agreed, to find money to introduce an advertising program to publicize the changes. I know he has shafted all the municipalities with respect to urban transit, but this particular matter I speak of is extremely important.
I must give the minister credit for a paper which he had prepared setting forth all the hypothetical questions and answers. I asked him and he agreed-he is nodding his head affirmatively so he thinks this is a good point-to find the money for an advertising campaign to let senior citizens know the effect of this bill, particularly those who will be taking advantage of the choices offered.
In amending the Old Age Security Act the minister had to refer to the spouse's allowance, much to his disappointment and chagrin. This is one of the most draconian and callous measures the government could possibly conceive. It is a very simple procedure, but the minister opened up a hornets' nest and has no sympathy for the people involved.
March 9, 1977

First of all, there are people living together-they do not even have to be married. They can be living in sin, but I do not want to get involved in that because we raised hell about it before. If the minister's morality leans that way, that is his business. If one spouse is 65 and the other spouse between 60 and 64-under 65-the younger is entitled to a spouse's allowance. The spouse's allowance was set up because it was recognized that two people could not live on one pension, so it was a good principle. But the minister goes along with the fact that when the person receiving the old age pension dies, the one receiving the spouse's allowance no longer gets it. If they are receiving a combined pension of $420 and the one on old age security dies, then the survivor gets nothing.
I do not know why the minister is so hard in this respect. His position is indefensible. There are 200 elderly people who get a message of condolence every month when the spouse dies but then we tell them they are not going to get any money and that they can go on welfare or social assistance. That is not the same thing, Mr. Speaker. Once a person receives an income as a right, which he or she will as a result of this legislation, then I cannot understand why the minister is insistent on cutting the survivor spouse's allowance off. That does not make sense; it is draconian; it is callous. I hope the minister will have second thoughts about this. He will probably give a lot of excuses, but we cannot accept them.
I should also point out that the spouse's allowance is discriminatory. The minister would be better advised to wait until he brings in social security legislation. If he thinks he can win the approval of the provinces to a guaranteed annual income, he would be better to wait until such time as the country can afford it, otherwise he will only alienate the senior citizens. Those between age 60 and 64 who are living with someone, married or not, are recognized, but widows, widowers, spinsters, bachelors and separated people in the same age group are left out. That is blatant discrimination and has no place in government policy. The principle is wrong and we on this side resent it. We shall continue to hammer home the fact that the death of one spouse should not disentitle the other. The minister is going to have to see to it that these people are recognized.
I think I have covered the important points, Mr. Speaker, and I know my colleagues will have something to say on the bill. It moves in the right direction. The old age security pension will now be based on periods of residence, and that is a good thing. When the bill is passed, the "all or nothing" law will be removed, and if a person desires he or she can acquire a portion of the pension. Some 500,000 people in the country will be affected by the new reciprocal agreements. There are countless hundreds concerned about pensions from Great Britain who have not been able to acquire either the escalation in the principal payment of the pension or the escalation itself. Once these agreements are entered into Canadians living abroad will be able to take advantage of the pension there and those who come here from abroad can take advantage of pensions they cannot draw now.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I indicated when I spoke on behalf of the New Democratic Party on second reading, we support the principle of this bill, which has the effect of establishing a new basis with respect to the residency requirements for old age security. That is still our position. Not only do we support it, we welcome it because we believe that what is being proposed will solve a number of problems and put things on a basis of fairness. However, I shall have something more to say about that in a few minutes.
Of course during the course of my remarks I shall say something about the things not in the bill and which ought to be in it. Likewise, I shall speak with strong feeling about one feature of the Old Age Security Act which is being continued by this legislation without any attempt to correct a flagrant injustice involved therein.
Having said that we support the change this bill will establish in the residency requirements, 1 think I should put on record again the motion this House passed under Standing Order 43 on Thursday, February 10, as reported on page 2905 of Hansard. I had the privilege of moving the motion. It was seconded by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander), and reads in these words:
That this House urges the media to make it clear to the people of Canada that anyone now in Canada who is 25 years of age or over will not be affected by the new rules regarding old age security but will, on reaching age 65, be able to qualify under the residence rules now in effect for the full amount of the basic pension.
Not only did the House pass the motion unanimously, but the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) read it into the record when the standing committee met to deal with the bill. He gave that plea his approval. Emphasizing this aspect of the matter at the beginning of one's speech may seem to be a bit of a departure from the broad principles of the legislation, but my experience and correspondence tell me that it must be emphasized.
Let me make it clear that I think many of the provisions in the new rules are good. 1 shall say why I think so in a moment. In the meantime many Canadians now in this country, when they hear about the new rules, are confused and concerned lest they will get less pension than they thought they would receive.
I think all in this House agree that we want it to be understood that anybody who is in Canada on the day this new law is proclaimed, which I understand is to be July 1, 1977, who is 25 years of age or older, still has the right to qualify under the old rules, because the law will provide precisely that any such person can choose as between the old rule and the new rule, whichever is to the benefit of that person. But even

March 9, 1977
Old Age Security
after we have settled these things and the press has reported them, we will still get letters and inquiries. People are concerned about these things. The minister says that he will give the matter publicity. I hope that that publicity, together with what we are saying, will relieve the anxiety of those now in the country who fear that something will happen to the amount of pension they will get.
The present full pension is available to anyone who has resided the last ten years before age 65 in Canada or who meets the various rules which can be substituted for that requirement. Such people will still be able to get the full pension.
Since I have said so much about the applicability of the old rules to those who are now in this country, why am I speaking favourably about the new rules; why do we bother with them? There are two main reasons for the new rules. First, they will make it possible for persons who have left Canada, or persons who leave Canada before age 65 and who at present, unless they go through a pretty awkward routine, get nothing, to get a proportional amount of the pension. The new rule says that you get one fortieth of the full pension for each full year of residency in Canada after age 18. That means that persons now abroad who are not able to draw the old age security pension will, under the new rules, if they spent 15, 20 or 30 years in Canada after age 18, be able to apply for a prorated portion of the old age security pension. It is unfortunate that many of these people have been denied pensions. I think the rule which made it possible for some individuals to get the pension by coming back and spending a year in Canada at age 64 or 65 was fair, but impossible for many people to meet. Sir, I think it is good that we are making this provision.
The other side of the coin is not so easy to defend initially; certainly it is not so easy to praise, because it suggests that certain persons may get a lesser pension. Those who might get less down the road sometime are persons who come to Canada after this bill becomes law and are here after age 18 for less than 40 years. They will get only that number of fortieths represented by the number of years they have been here after age 18. Since we do not pay the pension to those who have left, why should we not be fair and treat both those who have come and those who have gone away in the same way?
What is the rest of the picture? Under this law reciprocal arrangements will be possible with other countries, and as we gain experience with this new law we shall see that there will be a great many persons in Canada who will be drawing pensions made up of a portion earned while they were in Canada, and a portion earned while they were in some other country, or perhaps two or three other countries. I am satisfied that when this whole process is in full working order, in many of those cases the situation will be much better than now and that many individuals will have a better total pension than they can now receive. As I say, this matter must be based on fairness.
The thing that strikes me as unfair at the moment is this: A person can be born in this country and live here until he is 55 years of age and then go away; but unless he comes back for

that other year about which we all know, he gets nothing. On the other hand a person can come to this country at age 55 and ten years later get the full pension. Clearly, the all or nothing arrangement contains elements of unfairness. This legislation seeks to correct that unfairness, and in that respect we think it is a good idea.
I shall return to that in a moment. Before I do so may I say that in addition to the need to clear up the confusion existing in the minds of many who are now in this country, it will also be necessary to clear up the confusion which may arise once the new regime is in operation. I thank the hon. member for Hamilton West, a good friend, for making it unnecessary for me to include all that I might have put into my speech, by quoting what I said in the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs. I appreciate his compliment, that I made the case with the examples I gave. Actually, I gave two examples.
When the new rule comes into effect, some persons will get less than they would otherwise be entitled to if they apply at the wrong time. The scheme will be worked on the basis of full years. If a person applies when he has 29 years and 11 months of residency, he will get less than if he had waited another month, and had 30 years of residency. In other words, he would get twenty-nine fortieths instead of thirty fortieths. He should be advised to wait one more month.
Then there will be cases of those who, by waiting a year or two, might qualify under the old rule and get 100 per cent pension, whereas under the new rule they would get less. I am happy to say that the response we got in the standing committee to the two examples I raised was an assurance, especially from public service officials representing the department, that a counselling service for dealing with such cases will be established.
I testify to what the minister has said, that the regional old age security offices have been developing contacts with our constituency offices and that counselling services are more available than they used to be. I am glad to know that when the new system gets going there will be a still more active counselling service. It can be very important to a person whether he applies, say, this month or next. When you add the escalation factor, in the years down the road, the point at which a person applies can make a tremendous difference. It is no use applying and then realizing one should have waited a month. It is too late, then. The basic amount given is the basic amount for life. So I am glad this counselling is to be put in place.
The legislation, generally, is the kind we can support. The two elements of confusion we have been talking about, the confusion which exists right away on the part of those who are here, and the confusion which can come down the road a bit, need to be dealt with and I am glad the department intends to do so.
Despite the approval I have given to the change of residence rules, there is one element which disturbs me. I am not going
March 9, 1977

to make a big fuss about it today because I think the fuss will have to be made in ten or 11 years' time, so hon. members can count on me 10 or 11 years from now to raise the point I have in mind-provided some of them are still here!
We are saying that a year's residence in Canada after age 18 gives you a fortieth of the pension, whether you are born here or came as an immigrant, whatever the age was. That is complete mathematical fairness. But I also look at it this way: a person who lives in Canada until he is 35, 40, 50, pick any age you want, and who then goes away, has maybe taken a slightly different attitude than the person who comes here even as late as age 55. The ones who have gone away from Canada and left-in some cases it would be for health reasons; that is one of the main reasons why I am delighted about this bill- and in other cases it might be for economic reasons because they can pick up a pension or a higher income in some other way-have left the country, have shaken the dust of Canada off their shoes, but those who have come here have come by choice; they have decided they want to live here for the rest of their days. It may be just a bit tough to tell such persons that because they were here only ten or 15 years prior to age 55 they will get only ten or fifteen fortieths of the pension. The reason I am not unduly concerned about this is because I have been here long enough to know that when injustices of that kind develop something is usually done about them. This will not show up in the next 10 or 11 years.
During the next eight or nine years, the old rules will apply and the persons who come here late in life will not qualify under either set of rules. In about 10 or 11 years from now, you watch, there will be members getting up in this House and saying, "I have got correspondence, I have got cases of persons who have come here late in life, who have made this country their home, who have made a contribution, and some of them will get only ten or fifteen fortieths of the pension." And the minister over there will say ten or 15 years from now, "Oh, but that person can get the full GIS." And we will say from this side-or maybe we shall be over there-"Ten fortieths or fifteen fortieths of the basic pension and the full GIS don't add up to the amount he would get if he got the full pension, and the full GIS." And the minister of that day, if he is anything like the present minister, will say, "Oh, but such persons can apply for social assistance." Social assistance, relief, welfare, whatever you call it, still has a stigma attached to it no matter how much you say it is a right under the law. I believe that if the day comes when we realize that Canada is not being fair to some of our new Canadians, we shall correct it.
I say that, Mr. Speaker, because I remember the days when no pensions could be taken out of Canada at all. And then we got it so you could take it if you had been here for 25 years. Later we changed that to 20 years. I remember the days when missionaries who had spent their lives abroad could not get the pension in Canada. But, as these things came to light parliament had the decency to correct them. Therefore I believe that ten or 11 years from now, if it does become apparent that we are not being fair to the immigrants who have come to this country and have been here only ten or 15 years, we will at

that time do something about it. I would like to have it on the record now, and it comes from one who supports the bill, that this is a situation we may have to deal with a decade hence.

Listen! If you want me to make a speech about how the Liberals were forced to bring these things in, I shall do so. I have been here. I know the history. But I want to say to my hon. friends opposite who are now in a receptive mood and agreeing with me, that I see the day coming when retirement security, pensions for people generally will be based even more than they are today on the Old Age Security Act, and the Canada Pension Plan.
There is a great pension debate going on in the country right now. Do you know why that debate is going on? It is because private plans cannot fill the bill. Private plans cannot provide escalation, and all this campaign against escalation of public service pensions by private interests is just because they cannot do it.

Dr. Noel Hall in his report on railway pensions a while ago said that unless private pension plans can come through with escalation to keep pension plans up to the cost of living, they will fail. And I think they will. So I believe that what we need is to extend the Canada Pension Plan so that it provides not just 25 per cent of the income adjusted and so on of one's best working years, but 50 or 75 per cent.
Now I am back to what I was saying a moment ago when I was agreeing with my friends across the way that the concept of a basic flat pension, such as old age security, which is paid to everyone who reaches retirement age without any means test at all, plus an earnings-related pension on top of that, such as the Canada Pension Plan provides, is good. Not only is it good but it is the kind of thing that will provide the answer to failing private pension plans.
I completely support the position that is being taken by the Public Service Alliance of Canada in the advertising it has been spreading across the country these last few days to the effect that it is the private plans generally which are unfair to Canadians. Those who receive pensions from private pension plans represent only 40 per cent of the population of Canada. But who pays for them? The entire population.
We have a pension situation in Canada today in which everybody pays, but only some get good pensions. It would be far better to have everybody pay on an ability to pay basis, and everybody get adequate old age security under the Old Age Security Act and the Canada Pension Plan. I plead very strongly that we move in that direction and that we move fairly soon. These things can move faster than one believes.
I suppose I have said this before, but I can remember when 1 was a new, young member sitting in the back row advocating the removal of the means tests, advocating pensions of $30 a month when it was $20, and advocating a lowering of the age. Some of my Conservative friends who sat nearby would say to me, "You have a good and bright idea, Stanley, but it will never come about; you are too futuristic". We have gone beyond even my dreams when I first came here, Mr. Speaker. However, I am not dreaming now but I am being very realistic when I say that the kind of economy we have today, the whole business of pension funds and indexing, is such that the real challenge is for government to improve old age security, to extend the Canada Pension Plan, and to let these two be the main basis for retirement security for all our peoples.
I had better not forget to look at the clock now and again, Mr. Speaker, because there is something I do want to do before my time runs out. Again I want to thank the minister for one improvement which was put into the legislation, and that has to do with grandparents who are drawing OAS and GIS and also getting family allowance because they are bringing up their grandchildren. That has been taken care of in the legislation, but I still do not know why the minister could not have made this provision retroactive to cover the situation as of today. Here's hoping that somehow this will be done.

I welcome too his announcement today that the regulations respecting the right to have one's GIS based on the current year's income instead of the last year's will be revised so that most forms of income which cease will not have the effect of delaying an increase or causing a decrease in the guaranteed income supplement. I am glad that these steps have been taken.
This brings me to the last point, and by some strange coincidence it is the same subject the hon. member for Hamilton West spoke of at the end of his remarks this afternoon, namely, the spouse's allowance. I am glad to see the hon. member for York South (Mrs. Appolloni) in her seat this afternoon because I felt very encouraged by the stand she took on the spouse's allowance in a number of respects when we were dealing with this matter in the committee the other day. I noticed that the Minister of National Health and Welfare referred to one Liberal by name. He accepted his idea, but he referred to another Liberal member without giving her name because he had obviously not accepted her idea. When I say "his" and "her" that straightens it out, does it not?
The minister did answer one of the points made by the hon. member from York South, but I thought he brushed it aside with his usual capacity for not getting the point. My hon. friend from York South does not like the fact, because she is a woman and thinks that women should have equal rights, that a woman has to have her husband sign the application for spouse's allowance. I know it works both ways and the husband might have to ask the wife, but in most cases the wife is the younger spouse, and in practical terms this is the way it works out.
The minister says today that he has had his officials look at the matter and out of 75,000 applications there was only one case, says he, where spouse's allowance was not granted because the elder spouse would not sign the application. But the minister missed the point completely. It is not whether the couple gets the spouse's allowance; it is the indignity that the woman has to go through to get her husband, ornery though he may be, to sign the application.

I tried to make this point yesterday in a motion under Standing Order 43, to which the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) (Mrs. Campagnolo) said "Hear, hear" but to which others over there said "No", when I complained that it is contrary to the principles of equal rights and human justice, and all the rest of it, to say to a woman between the age of 60 and 65 that she cannot get a pension unless she produces a husband. In other words, neither a spinster nor a widow qualifies.
This whole set-up is totally wrong. I am delighted that the hon. member for Hamilton West concentrated on it as he did in the latter part of his speech, and I was pleased with the stand which the hon. member for York South took on the matter in committee the other day. But no matter how you slice it, Mr. Speaker, the fact of the matter is that the government is saying to persons between 60 and 65 that, in
March 9, 1977

addition to a means test, they have to undergo a marital test. If you have a husband or a wife and you meet the other two conditions, you get the allowance; if you do not have a husband, or if you are a man and you do not have a wife, you do not get it.
The minister says that his aim was to solve the problem of two people trying to live on one pension. When we come back and tell him that if that is impossible, how can he expect one person to live on no pension, his reply is that social assistance is also a right. I hope that we made our point in committee. This is the line that can be taken in the comfort of the House of Commons, or in the comfort of the committee room or the minister's office, but out there in Canada people who have to apply for social assistance, relief, or welfare, feel it is a stigma, that there is shame attached to it. What they want is a pension as of right.
The minister also says that I am trying to use the back door to get pensions at 60. I do not care whether it is the back door, the side door, the front door, or coming down the chimney, the fact is that I do want pensions available at 60. I am satisfied to have them available between the age of 60 and 65 for those out of the labour market. I think that is a reasonable test. But to have a marital test and to say to a woman that she does not qualify for a pension unless she has a husband is completely contrary to the Bill of Rights.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker, but I am enjoying the help. I am not so concerned about pensions that are paid in common law situations because in many cases there are explanations. But if the allowance is paid to both spouses, under common law, surely it can be paid to spinsters and widows.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, I am glad the hon. member for York South got into this question the other day. My hon. friend from Hamilton West raised the question, where was she in 1975? Most Canadians did not realize this in 1975. We did. The hon. member for Hamilton West, the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald), and some of the rest of us fought hard several years ago to try to get something done. As months went on and people became aware of it, they were horrified. Even newspapers now carry editorials expressing horror at this sort of thing. I think the whole question ought to be reviewed, and before I sit down I shall give the House a chance to vote on a motion that would call for the whole question of the spouse's allowance to be reviewed.
It is wrong to deny the spouse's allowance to a spinster or widow. I would give it to everyone in that bracket who is out of the labour market. That is my position, and everyone knows it. But it seems to me that it is the ultimate in cruelty and meanness to say to a wife who is 62 or 63 and is on the
Old Age Security
spouse's allowance that, when her 67 or 68 year old husband dies, her spouse's allowance will be cut off. According to statistics, that is happening to about 200 Canadians a month. There is no defence for it at all. That phase of the matter should be reviewed, and reviewed seriously right away.
The minister is quite right when he says I want to go further. I want pensions available to all at age 60 who are out of the labour market. As a lifetime opponent of means tests, it will be hard for me to say that I will accept some kind of income test for anyone between 60 and 65. However, the test I cannot accept is a marital test. It is just not fitting and I feel that this House should say so.
After all the kind things I have said about my friend from York South, and I appreciate what she did in committee the other day, I hope that she will get into this and give her support at this stage.

The Tories did a little, but most of it has been Liberal legislation. However, every last bit of it was because the Liberals were prodded from this side of the House right from the beginning. The reason we on this side are still prodding is because we believe it will work. We believe we will yet get pensions at 60, certainly between 60 and 65 for all those out of the labour market. If that cannot be done in this session, we will have to go a step at a time. If, for example, when we bring down the pension age we have to do it from 65 to 64, to 63, to 62, to 61, to 60, that is fine. However, there is one thing we can surely bring an end to right away, that is, cutting off the pension and the allowance of the spouse who becomes a widow before she reaches 65.
When we were debating veterans affairs the other day, I told the story of the wife of a veteran in New Brunswick. The veteran is on a 15 per cent disability pension, old age security, the guaranteed income supplement, and war veterans allowance. As she is about to turn 60, she has been told she must apply for the spouse's allowance. That is the way the law reads. She will get the spouse's allowance, the veteran's allowance will be cut off and they will be right where they were in terms of dollars.
This woman has asked what will happen if her husband dies before she is 65. She will be out of everything. His disability pension drops because it is less than 48 per cent, the old age security drops, the guaranteed income supplement drops, and

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, now that the matter is settled between the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander), I would like to add a few words about that amendment to the Old Age Security Act. I am convinced that hon. members will not show any partisanship. I would not want for any reason whatever to make a political football out of our senior citizens. It does not matter whether the legislation is amended under a Liberal, Progressive Conservative, New Democractic or Social Credit government. What matters is for parliament to assume its responsibilities and give senior citizens this right to security. Moreover, if we consider mankind, we will realize that any human being seeks security from birth till death. Consider a baby in his crib, he is concerned for his security. He cries when he is apprehensive.
Most of the time, since it is the mother who looks after the children, the child will turn to her and call out: Mother! This means that something is bothering him and that he feels insecure.

Let us also observe, a little later, the student. When children start attending school, whether it be kindergarten, primary or secondary school, college or university, at all levels, they worry about security. They want some security. They want to be assured that their life will be trouble free and that their needs will be met.
Let us look a little later at teenagers, when they begin to feel a responsible part of society. Then they want absolute security. They work to secure it for themselves. And when they become adults and enter the labour market, let us consider all the labour demands and everything the unions will do to obtain security for their membership. This is further evidence that everybody is concerned with security.
All through his life, Mr. Speaker, a person works to ensure his security and to make sure that in his old age, when he is no longer able to work and earn a living, he will have the money and the income required to support himself. It is in this respect, Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) so rightly said a while ago, that Canada has a social security scheme which is quite advanced and provides eligible senior citizens with the security they need. One only has to look to the south at the United States, and extremely powerful nation, to realize that our old age security pension scheme is superior to theirs. Which does not mean that we must rest on our laurels and show complacency instead of trying to improve this scheme within the possibilities available in Canada.
Again last weekend, I received representations from senior citizens, from people who are not yet 60 but who are having a hard time finding a job so as to be self-sufficient. I was told by the way that the most difficult time in life is between 50 and 65, because there is no quaranteed security. One cannot be sure of having a job or a guaranteed monthly or yearly income. So this is a period of insecurity, the most difficult period in life.
Mr. Speaker, even though I support the principle of the bill, even though I am pleased with the amendments designed to make the act more equitable for a larger number of people, whether they be immigrants or people who had to leave the country and return after a number of years, I feel such improvements are desirable and deserve to be supported, promoted and implemented. But the fact remains that under the act as it is now, Mr. Speaker, the pension is granted to people of 60 who are living with another person of 65 or more.
When this legislation was passed, 1 recall very well making comments in the Elouse and urging the Minister of National Health and Welfare to amend the bill so as to respect the sacredness of marriage. Under this legislation, ever since its enactment there is no need to be married to be eligible for old age security. You only need to be 60 years of age, to live with a person of 65 without necessarily being married-to shack up-but to have been seen with an older person aged 65 or more. As I said then, I think this flies in the face of the divine institution that is family.
Old Age Security
In fact, a family is composed of a husband, a wife and finally, when the circumstances are favourable, of children. But at 65, being husband and wife is just the same as on the day of marriage at age 20. The unfortunate thing in all this are representations, for example, like those made to me again last weekend, namely that when someone is aged 60, 62 or 63 and his spouse in wedlock or otherwise is 65, 66 or 68 and the later dies, the surviving spouse is left without a pension. That person loses everything and has to rely on welfare, a worse situation than before. Mr. Speaker, I submit to the minister that we should amend the act once more to authorize payment of the spouse's allowance to persons under 65 even where the qualifying pensioner has died, so as to prevent difficult situations.
This often has serious consequences not only for the person involved but also for his or her family. Because when someone has been counting on a guaranteed income and that income suddenly disappears, this creates very serious difficulties. That person must go on welfare and God knows, Mr. Speaker, it is not an easy matter these days to need welfare because regulations get tougher and tougher, they are implemented in a much tighter way than they used to be. It seems that the tougher the situation, the more stringently regulations are applied. A very great number of people are now in almost destitute circumstances, and it is an anomaly that in Canada we should be imposing in 1977 impossible circumstances on people in that age group.
It must be recognized that in general people 60 and over have been doing hard work all their lives, they have tried to earn a living, they contributed to Canada's development, building parishes, towns, cities and industries, day after day, through their work with their fellow citizens, in the hope that when they became disabled or older, society would recognize their contribution to Canada as a whole and that well-earned security would be generously forthcoming. Work is the reason for our being on earth, it is a gift of Providence. Working is fine, working is rewarding: that is what makes us achieve something, provided we get something out of it not only for today but also for tomorrow when there will be fewer paydays and as physical strength will start going down.
Mr. Speaker, I think the government is moving gradually in the right direction, but they should proceed much more quickly because the more they wait, the worse it gets. When changes are made, it is very often too late; the damage is done, the conditions have changed and our solutions are obsolete, because we live in a sick society.
My hon. friend opposite is smiling at me, as if I were telling him a cock-eyed story. However, I know that in a constituency like mine, just as in all the other ridings in Canada, there are hardship cases which give the shivers to those responsible for running a large and beautiful country like Canada, a country able to provide those of 60 and over with some security without their having to go through all kinds of procedures they know practically nothing about.

Yes, the minister of health or his officials; they work hand in hand, I believe. Information is enclosed in the envelopes with the pension cheques. I would ask him to see to it that this information is more explicit, more specific and detailed, so that these people may know where and to whom they should write to have a situation corrected.
I have already said it and I repeat it today. In the province of Quebec, in the district office for the Quebec area, at least those responsible for the old age security pensions and family allowances are competent. They get busy whenever you show them that a situation needs to be corrected.
Mr. Speaker, I wish I could pay the same compliment to all departments, all civil servants. Unfortunately, that is impossible. In some departments, the minister's instructions are completely ignored, civil servants could not care less about the authorities and the recommendations of hon. members who are delegated and elected by their fellow citizens; all these things are overlooked, ignored, those people could not care less.
That is why in Canada, at the present time, there exists in some groups a dissatisfaction which makes us shudder, which annoys and worries us; we should all together take a serious look into what is going on and work together, so that our fellow citizens, Canadians, both Francophones and Anglophones, can say that in Canada the administration is responsible and does everything in its power to give equal opportunities to all Canadians from all parts of the country.
Mr. Speaker, if we give ourselves the trouble of doing this all together, we will have made much progress and will make even more in coming months: time is of the essence. Mr. Speaker, it makes me boil to see ministers, civil servants and senators go on television on the French network of the CBC and say they are concerned about national unity, about the fate of Canada. But they are the ones who got us into this mess, by their laissez-faire, free and easy attitude. And now, throwing their arms up in the air, they cry out: Something must be done, the ship is going to sink.
Mr. Speaker, the time to act is not after the ship has been abandoned but while we are still aboard so we can row and get the ship in to port. Mr. Speaker, no wonder the ship of Canadian unity is drifting and many serious people are showing great concern about this. It is because we did not take our responsibilities when it was time to do so. Two or three weeks ago I raised a point during the adjournment motion at ten o'clock.
I submitted the idea that we should consider the possibility of granting pensions at 60, of lowering the age of early retirement for all those who want to leave the labour market and would then receive the OAS pension. The minister answered-which was quite expectable-by saying that there

are thousands of unemployed people, housewives and forcibly retired people who are without work but who would still want to have this pension.
Mr. Speaker, to that I say they should sit down and seriously consider the appropriate statistics so as to figure out just how many people of 60 are on a payroll-men or women-and how many of those people pay into a retirement fund of any kind. Let them find out how many people would be willing to retire voluntarily to be able to do something else. And I do know that at 65 they are not all finished, I know there are still people able to work, to be efficient and useful in their environment, in their country, and that is why I want them to have that freedom to continue to work or retire. I am not thinking of something autocratic, dictatorial, but a voluntary thing.
Mr. Speaker, I think that after considering all those figures I am convinced you will find that Canada would be in a much better position to give them that security and allow young people who want to work to do so. There are still young people who want to work-my office is flooded every week with young people who come to my office to ask their member of parliament to help them find a job because they want to work-and I would much rather help them find a job than help them get unemployment insurance or social welfare benefits. Before 25, 30, 40, it is not time to live on pensions, it is time to build. But at 60 it is time to reap, to benefit from one's effort.
The government, the state, all together we should make an effort considering the rate of unemployment and the great number of unemployed who do not produce anything but to whom we must pay unemployment insurance or social welfare benefits to allow them to live. I think it would be right to tell older people: at 60, you have earned it, you have worked hard, the government is amending its legislation and is going to allow you to retire voluntarily at 60. And each of those people could be given a well deserved old age security. Mr. Speaker, in three or four months you would notice the change in this country because I know from my experience there are in my underdeveloped area of the south shore many people who find it rough, who barely make it, who do not have all the necessary income to allow them to face their daily needs and who would like very much to be able to enjoy the advantages of their country.
However, there are many young men and young women who have nothing to do and who would like to make some contribution. Mr. Speaker, it is not difficult to speak to young people, they are people like everyone else. I raised twelve of them and I never hesitated to speak to them and reprimand them when need be. They did not hate me for all that, and all the members who have children know it. We must make young people understand that in society they have both rights and obligations and that they must accept them if they really want their rights to be respected. They must start by doing their duty, and then demand that their rights be respected.
When we tell this to young people, they understand us and they end up by recognizing that we are right and by understanding that there must be a time in life to build, a time to
March 9, 1977

develop, a time to sow and a time to reap, and that the time to reap is not when you are 20. It comes many years later. This is why I say that the time to reap has come for the people aged 60, and I am glad to hear serious people like the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander), the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and all hon. members, whatever their party, who have the same ideas and who want to work towards the same end so that we may pass a legislation which will respect the sacred character of the family and of marriage and which will still grant the right to security to any single person. It is not necessary to be married; people should receive old age security at 60 instead of having to live hypocritically with someone else to qualify immediately for old age security. The present legislation is terrible if we think about this and if we want to go to the bottom of things.
Mr. Speaker, I make this plea once again with all the strength that I have and with all the heart that God has given me. I urge the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) and all members of parliament to allow this legislation to be amended to make it as good as it can possibly be. Moreover, I believe that the amendment suggested by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is intelligent and logical. It is not a matter of thinking about things which do not exist and I would not like to see tomorrow's newspapers reporting to Canadians that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has moved an amendment to kill the bill. This is not the case and it is not in this spirit that the amendment has been moved. What is the substance of the amendment? That the bill be referred to the committee to be studied again and amended so that it truly meets the needs of this category of persons, whether they be married, widowed, bachelors or whatever; the only important requirement is to be 60 years of age.
Mr. Speaker, nobody can give us a guarantee that in two, three or five years, the legislation will not be amended again so that the age of eligibility for old age pension will again be reduced by a few years. That is evolution, evolution in the right direction, evolution toward ever better social, economic and financial benefits based on work and on a common will to work toward progress from one year to another.
Now, Mr. Speaker, while I accept the underlying principle of this bill, there are some improvements which I think should be made. By the way, if you would allow me to make my point I think that by tomorrow most members would share my view on the matter. It often happens here that motions are moved under Standing Order 43 which requires the unanimous consent of the House to have them put and although 264 members, that is 262 excluding the Chair may agree, if one shakes his head in dissent, the Speaker sees him and forgets all the others. Such are our standing orders! It is that much out-of-date.
It is not necessary to hear someone say no, he only has to shake his head in dissent and the motion cannot be put. However, under Standing Order 28, it is provided that any member who wants to speak in the House must rise and ask the permission of the Chair. To say no to a motion is saying something. So why not observe the rules? Why not rise and
Old Age Security
say: I object to this so that one's name will be recorded in the official report?
Mr. Speaker, I think that those few remarks that I made in good faith, in all honesty, in the interest of my country, will be favourably received and that the committee responsible for changing the procedures will take them into account, as it is an obsolete rule, and one should have the courage of one's convictions. If you do not want to give your unanimous consent, you should rise and say no. I think that all members would be pleased if we abided by the decision of the hon. member who said no.
Mr. Speaker, in conclusion, I ask again the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde), whom I consider as a gentleman, as a man aware of his responsibilities, to reflect further on the modest remarks I made on behalf of those people who truly deserve well of their country, who are in need, who are worried in the most difficult period of their life because they lose their strength, they still have the same needs but they get no income. Those people are worried and have difficult years when we could offer them a much happier life.
I think it should be the contribution of young people to those persons who built roads, schools, industries which allow them to have a better standard of living. It is for young people that we have devoted our life and it is the same process from one generation to the next. If the following generation succeeds better than we did we shall be very happy. I shall be the first to say: You achieved more than we did. But as we did everything we could, give us at least the chance in our old age to do more without worrying about our vital needs.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I will be brief. Obviously all members of the House would like to improve social benefits in all areas. That is understandable, easy to propose and to push for when you are in opposition and do not have responsibility for spending public funds.

speechtext:
The House has heard the proposal for lowering the eligibility age to 60. This would mean an additional expenditure in 1977 alone for OAS, GIS and the CPP retirement program of some $2,035 million. That sum would be made up as follows: roughly $1.5 billion would be spent on OAS, $450 million on GIS, and $86 million on the Canada Pension Plan. That is the kind of money we are discussing.
We made certain proposals to the provinces in the course of the social security review. The House has been asked to consider the difficulties of those between the age of 60 and 65 only. I suggest that the problem of poverty in this country is far broader than that. At present, those in need in this country can be looked after by provincial assistance programs, to which the government contributes 50 per cent of the cost under the Canada Assistance Plan.

March 9, 1977
Old Age Security
In the course of the social security review, we have proposed to the provinces a form of guaranteed income which would cover income support for those unable to work, whatever their age. It would cover those unable to work, whatever their age. It would cover those who are 59, 58, and 57 years old, as well as those between the ages of 60 and 65. We have proposed a program of income supplementation, a program to supplement the incomes of those still able to work and earn a living even though forced to downgrade their activities and earn a lower income than when they were active and in the prime of life. The provinces support this broad concept. We are looking at methods of implementing such a program. I hope that by the end of this year we shall have concluded reviews of techniques for administering such an approach. The provinces endorse this concept in principle. However, several provinces have indicated that they may not have the resources in the next few years with which to provide such a program to their citizens.
We are considering if in any way we can speed up the implementation of this program, either by the provinces or through the federally administered income tax system. I suggest that this proposal would be the best solution to poverty in this country. It has the advantage of being flexible, in the sense that those who want to continue working and are able to work will see their incomes improved. At the same time it is a characteristic of the program that it will be able to answer the needs of people, whatever their age.
I suggest that the patchwork proposal put forward this afternoon by the opposition is merely another band-aid; it will not deal broadly enough with the general poverty problem in this country. We, on my side of the House, are just as concerned as any hon. members opposite about poverty in this country.

speechtext:
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) said that he recognized that most of the social legislation of this country has been brought in at the initiative of Liberal governments. That has been the case in the past, and I am convinced it will remain so in years to come. We have no lesson to learn from anybody. I think our record in this respect bears examination by the citizens of this country, and that is exactly what the citizens of this country have been examining regularly, at election times.
If the amendment comes to a vote, I shall vote against it. I think that it is not a progressive suggestion. The proposal is just another piece of patchwork. I think the answer clearly lies in the area of a general program of income support and supplementation.
The whole question of retirement has become much more complex than some hon. members this afternoon have indicated. People in this country are living longer and longer, and more and more people would like to keep on working. At present there is pressure in many areas from people over 65 who have been forced to retire. They complain that they are forced to retire at 65, but would like to continue working and earning a living. They do not want to be forced to retire as

they are forced to do at present, thanks to the provisions of private and public pension plans which make pensions available at 65. Many academics and specialists in old people's problems argue that we should consider introducing greater flexibility to our private and public pension systems.
The fact is that if we lower pensions to age 60, we shall see a repetition of what happened when we lowered the pension age to 65. Hon. members may remember that the universal pension was paid at age 70. When we began paying pensions on a selective basis to those aged 65, there was so much pressure from the public and private sectors to retire people at 65 that we ended up paying the universal pension at age 65. Employers and organizers of private pension schemes then made sure people retired at age 65, and they were forced out of the labour market. There is no reason to think that people will not be forced out of the labour market at age 60 in years to come, if we pay the old age pension at age 60 strictly on a universal basis. These factors must be considered independently of the additional $2 billion and increasing annual additional expenditure which would be necessary if the proposal were implemented. It is our responsibility to tell the Canadian public how and where we shall raise the money. Frankly, the opposition has not justified the argument on either ground.
I think the wave of the future will be a form of guaranteed income for the citizens of this country. It will be a two-tier system of income support for those unable to work, and a system of income supplementation for those who can work but do not earn enough to meet their needs. The government has proposed this, is working on it, and will bring it before the House in due course.
I suggest that the proposal of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is a reactionary approach to this particular issue, and not worthy of support.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, being the member of parliament from Victoria where I have 19,600 old age pensioners in my constituency gives me more than a passing interest in this subject.
I listened with interest to the minister's remarks and I noticed the same omission as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) when the minister wished to point out how expensive old age pensions were. He included CPP, OAS, GIS and everybody over 60, and said how much it would cost. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre rightly pointed out that these were not the people we were talking about in this amendment. What we are talking about are the spouses, or the so-called spouses mentioned in the act, particularly in Clauses 8 and 9. A quick estimation is that if there are 200 who come on at the median age of 62'/2, each month they lose about $200 a month, which comes to about $40,000, and if you multiply that by 2Vi years you get a fairly reasonable figure, nothing like $2 billion, not even a tenth of $2 billion. It is rather misleading to pretend when speaking to this amendment that we are talking about a $2 billion load on the taxpayer. The minister had the gall, I suppose that would be the word, to say the opposition was taking a band-aid approach and that these were patchwork amendments. This is not so at all. I suspect the minister speaks with a great deal of knowledge when he talks about band-aid approaches.
It is interesting to follow the history of Bill C-35. It has come from an announcement made almost a year ago by the minister that he intended to bring in a bill to make reciprocity of pensions possible in Canada. He made that statement last April. It takes a while to get used to the habit the government has of making announcements, and I suppose every time government ministers think they are going to bring in a good bill you can usually count on four or five special announcements about it. First, they announce they are going to bring it in, and then a month or so later they announce they are going to bring it in fairly quickly. And a couple of months later you get another announcement, with more and more fanfare with each announcement, and the third one will probably say they are going to bring it in almost immediately and it is already printed and waiting for the proper time. Then they start announcing they are trying to get it on their own order paper. Eventually, after ten months of prodding by the opposition to produce this bill, the minister finally produced it.
The bill is divided roughly into two main parts, the part dealing with partial pensions, and the part dealing with reciprocal pensions.
Old Age Security
The part dealing with partial pensions is so complicated that I can hardly see how any ordinary person could forecast some of the questions that the bill will provoke. He will certainly not be able to tell the answers to some of the questions the bill will raise by way of partial pensions.
My hon. friend from Hamilton West and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre have drawn attention to the difficulties which will arise in making a sound financial judgment when a prospective pensioner reaches the age of 65 and qualifies under one or more of these schemes to draw a pension or a partial pension. It may well be there will be cases, as has been pointed out in committee, when a would-be recipient reaches the age of 65 and qualifies for a partial pension, that if he waits another year or two years he could qualify for a full pension. This is probably a simple matter for a person of private means, a retired member of parliament or cabinet minister, or anyone who is able to manage his own affairs successfully in the cut and thrust world we live in. He could soon work out how much he would be likely to draw if he waited for the full pension. He could then determine whether it was a good move to wait for the pension or to draw the partial pension.
It is interesting to think about what will happen to a person drawing a partial pension. You reach age 65 and are qualified for the minimum partial pension; you get a pension in 1977 dollars of $35 a month. It is as simple as that. It is a quarter of what you would get if you had a full pension, which at the present time is $140 a month. The granting of a partial pension is going to cause severe problems. It is going to lock in a new class of poverty-stricken pensioners. The minister knows full well that giving them a partial pension and the full guaranteed income supplement will not be a complete answer. We will have a couple drawing full pension and full GIS, getting $424 a month, but if another couple are drawing a quarter pension they get much less than that. If they draw a quarter of a pension, how are they to survive, because the figure of $424 is arrived at for a couple to enable them to sustain life and be sheltered? It is not there to permit any luxuries at all. It represents a basic pension.
The Ministry of National Health and Welfare has worked it out that it takes $424.74 to sustain the life of a couple. Now we are to have a new class who come in and instead of getting $141 a month each they are to get a much lower figure. They will get a quarter of the basic pension, $70, plus $160, which is $230 a month, on which to live. These people will go through our social assistance programs and welfare programs and be checked out very thoroughly. Remember, the government has already decided the basic necessity level of couples at $424. Yet this couple are expected to live on considerably less. This will create an additional problem.
The second part of the bill covers reciprocal pensions. This is a move in the right direction. For several years we have been asking for reciprocal pensions with other nations. Many of our friends and nations around the world have entered into agreements with each other providing for reciprocal pensions. Up until recently the only answer we could get from the Minister

March 9, 1977
