of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) was that Canada was quite willing but we could not find any other countries which would agree, and this was holding us up. If that was truly the case there would be no need for this bill at all. The minister now says that we need this bill to make this possible and I am glad to oblige him, if he can manage to get the bill through the House.
There are a couple of points I want to make concerning reciprocal pensions. Those in desperate need of reciprocal pensions are people who live in countries whose currency has recently been devalued in terms of purchasing power. I think particularly of people from the United Kingdom. Consider the fate of a couple who came here, say, five years ago with a pension income of 100 pounds sterling a month each, which in those days would have been a respectable amount on which to retire. Every month their pound becomes worth less, it seems, and every month the cost of Canadian food increases. The result of these two factors is that their standard of living declines at twice the rate. We have to think of these people, and we welcome the move toward reciprocal pensions as provided in this bill.
We hope that reciprocal pensions will come into effect as quickly as possible. The minister assured us in committee that some other countries are quite interested. France, Britain and Italy have already inquired about setting up a reciprocal agreement. One would hope that the minister will pursue these agreements without waiting until the date of July 1, and perhaps have the agreements made effective the day the bill is proclaimed.
Another matter respecting reciprocal pensions about which I worry considerably is the narrow group to which they apply. 1 am speaking, of course, of old age security pensions. The bill does not make provision for veterans pensions to be made reciprocal, nor for war disability pensions immigrants receive from their home country. I hope that the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) will take note of this and to his best to bring in a bill similar to this making it possible for veterans of forces in other countries who come to Canada to bring their pensions with them.
Another aspect concerning this bill which has not been discussed relates to the number of countries from whom we have received immigrants over the years, particularly in the last two years, which have no pension system at all. These people will not, of course, benefit from this bill. This means we will have a class of people who qualify for reciprocal pensions, mainly people coming from western Europe and the United States, and those who cannot bring any pension with them. Here I think particularly of people from the sub-continent and from Asia where pensions appear to be unknown.
Finally, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has moved an amendment to this bill. I suggest our party would have presented the same amendment, except we were a little more worried than the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre about delaying the bill. We understand that the bill

will be back here tomorrow if it is not passed today, and under those circumstances it removes the last reason, really the only reason, that we might have had to vote against the amendment.
Certainly we take second place to no one in our dislike of Clauses 8 and 10. These amendments would authorize the payment of partial spouse's allowances, based on the number of years that a spouse has resided in Canada after age 18, and would replace the present "all or nothing" system over a 40 year transitional period. The new sub-section will render ineligible for a spouse's allowance a person who is in Canada illegally.
For the benefit of those interested in women's rights and women's liberation, I notice on page 8 of the bill reference to the spouse as a "he". Proposed Section 17.1 requires the spouse of a pensioner to reside in Canada, and "if he does not reside in Canada", is not separated from the pensioner. Perhaps we will have to use impersonal pronouns rather than personal pronouns because it does make the situation a little confusing in regard to whether a pensioner or a spouse is not required to be separated from the pensioner.
This is a peculiar provision which is causing the government a great deal of trouble. The trouble is self-inflicted. When the original bill was brought in permitting spouse's allowances, the government did what my colleague from Hamilton West described as a dastardly act in providing that while a husband and a wife, one of whom was over 65, needed $282.68 plus $160.06, for a total of $442.74, to live on, as soon as one died the survivor would need no money at all. This is a peculiar kind of arithmetic, the sort I suppose you get into in cabinet when you are dealing with nothing less than $1 million for a while. I am sure it is difficult for them to understand that while it is easy to get the computer to work it all out, it is impossible for a survivor to survive on nothing.
I realize that there are a lot of regulations which will result from the passage of this bill, and members of parliament and the general public are not able to wade through them all. But the bill itself has some very peculiar omissions. For example, since a person must not be separated from the pensioner, I am curious as to what happens if a pensioner sets up a menage a trois and then kicks his wife out of the home, or vice versa, and cohabits with the survivor of the three. Then after a period of time the interloper in this household starts drawing spouse's allowance while the duly married wife is out in the cold, unable to make an application because she is separated from the pensioner. It seems to me that this is the way the bill presently reads. It is no wonder that the minister gets a little upset when we try to discuss this particular provision.
This is another reason why we want to discuss the bill and the clauses dealing with spouses. We want to discuss the outrageous attitude taken toward a widow or widower who not only has to go through the traumatic experience of losing husband or wife, but who then has the minister's bill telling him or her immediately after the funeral that the survivor needs no money and will get none from the federal government. This will be a shock, and is an affront to all of us. For
March 9, 1977

sheer meanness, Mr. Speaker, it can only be classed with the action of the Minister of Veterans Affairs, who managed to bring in a bill to pay an annual gratuity to ex-prisoners of war in World War II but who denies the same thing to veterans of World War I. I guess they are getting pretty old now; there are not too many of them left so the government does not worry about their votes.
When we were discussing this bill in committee, two things stood out. I asked the minister if poor people who needed money through a partial pension, and who really would be much better off waiting a further period of time until they qualified for a full pension, would have sufficient counselling to the effect that they would be advised to wait. Such people may need the money desperately. If they succumb to the temptation of a partial pension, what happens two years later when they come back and say that they made a terrible mistake and desperately need the full pension? The minister in his rather authoritarian manner said absolutely not, no retroactive choice will be permitted. This will cause nothing but trouble. It may not happen to somebody in the economic bracket in which the minister finds himself, but it will happen. People at age 65 are not going to be able to resist getting further income if they have a need.
When I asked the minister about this, he said they could go on welfare. There have been euphemisms for welfare for centuries. It was first called charity, then the dole and relief during the thirties and forties. It then became welfare, and is now called social assistance. It does not fool anyone. As far as the recipient is concerned, it is still welfare. The recipient knows that if you can get a pension, you can hold up your head. If you go on welfare, it is rather more difficult to do that.
This reminds me of the story of the school teacher who teaches singing. By the end of the day the children are separated into three groups, canaries, robins, and magpies. The kids know what is wrong with the magpies, they cannot sing well. The minister who speaks kindly of social assistance knows that it is a heck of a lot different than getting a pension to which everyone knows they are entitled.
I do not want to take much time. I am pleased that the bill has finally made it here. I hope we will soon see it put through. I ask the minister to bear in mind that we have taken this unusual action at this stage of the proceedings, supporting a motion to send the bill back to committee, because clauses 8 and 9 are so abhorrent. We are willing to wait an extra bit of time to see that they are removed or replaced with something that does not pick at the widow or widower, which this bill seems to do.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege to say one thing. I am very pleased that the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) did get to his feet. However, I can say this. The only people in this House whom 1 do not trust are those who sit on the government side.

subsubtopic: SIXTY-FIVE YEARS OF AGE AND OVER CONTINGENT UPON RESIDENCE IN CANADA
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: SIXTY-FIVE YEARS OF AGE AND OVER CONTINGENT UPON RESIDENCE IN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I submit that rather than a question of privilege that is a point of debate. It does not take away from the observation made by my colleagues and myself, and perhaps even some of those across the way. It appeared as though there was a lack of trust between two parties in this debate. One party complained that it had not been given the confidence of the other with regard to the intention of the NDP to move a motion. That is a legitimate observation, and it will be seen on the record tomorrow.
There is a second observation or conclusion one has to make when sitting on this side of the House. It is with regard to the contradictory policies of the opposition parties, particularly Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition. Today the spokesman for the official opposition asked for more and better pensions. But almost every second day their financial critic asks the government to reduce taxes. How can that kind of an approach be reconciled? I suggest that the hon. member for Hamilton West get together with the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) and decide on an approach.
It does not take a financial genius to realize that if you want to improve pensions, social security programs, and do more for Canadians, you cannot ask Canadians to pay less taxes. Even a child in grade five would understand that elementary principle of arithmetic.
Today we have another typical example of the Official Opposition speaking from both sides of their mouths. During the question period the hon. member for York-Simcoe asked for a reduction in taxes. During the debate on Bill C-35, another hon. member asked for more and better pensions. How can you possibly reconcile this forked-tongued approach on the part of the Official Opposition?
I will not develop this theme any further because we all respect the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and the fine contribution he has made over the decades he has been here. He was here one hundred years before me, and he will be here one hundred years after me!

subsubtopic: SIXTY-FIVE YEARS OF AGE AND OVER CONTINGENT UPON RESIDENCE IN CANADA
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: SIXTY-FIVE YEARS OF AGE AND OVER CONTINGENT UPON RESIDENCE IN CANADA
speechtext:
When it comes to pensions, we all know that the hon. member has his heart in the right place, even though in some cases his arithmetic may not be the strongest. In any event, we love him and think that he has fine qualities.
This bill has several elements. It introduces an element whereby a resident of Canada can gradually earn his pension through a period of residence in this country. This is welcomed

and supported by Canadians in general. It has another element which is a positive feature. It gives the minister power to enter into negotiations with other nations from whom we receive immigrants, and nations to which Canadians sometime emigrate. This is good.
I suppose that Canadians in other nations will benefit as well as immigrants to Canada from countries such as Italy, Portugal, Greece, the West Indies, South America, Asia, Africa, and other parts of the world. As a result of this bill the minister and the government will be empowered to enter into negotiations with those countries. We will have an element that already exists in western European countries, namely, the totalization of pensions.
A worker may have contributed for a few years as an immigrant in Brazil, a few years as an immigrant in France, a few years in Great Britain, Scandinavia, the United States, and finally comes to Canada. He will at last have an opportunity to see the contributions that he made in those countries throughout his working life recognized in the form of a pension that will be paid to him as a result of his contributions. This is something that does not exist today in North America. It does exist at least within the European Common Market countries as a result of reciprocal arrangements. This is a good, positive, fine Liberal measure.
Therefore, in connection with this bill, I am concerned with only one aspect, and some hon. members who have spoken before me have addressed themselves to this question-and that is the case of those people who have not earned credits in other countries before coming to Canada and who may well come here when the new law will be in full effect, when, years from now, some of us will no longer be around, people who, on coming to Canada, may seek employment for the first time when they are in their forties or their fifties and may not therefore have contributed to the Canada Pension Plan until late in life. At the age of retirement, whatever it may be at that time, they will not qualify except for the amount corresponding to the number of years that they will have resided in Canada.
Let us say an immigrant who will come here at the age of 50 will, at the age of 65, have been 15 years in the labour market and have contributed for that number of years out of the total 40 years required to receive a full pension. If that immigrant has no other income, he will qualify for a guaranteed income supplement. What I would like to make sure, through this intervention, Mr. Speaker, is whether he will qualify, in the case, for instance, of the program called Gains in Ontario which is under the Canada Assistance Plan, for the additional income that may be provided under that program.
What I would like to make sure is that ten, 15, or 20 years from now the totality of old age security, plus the guaranteed income supplement, plus the provincial supplement-which may vary from province to province such as Ontario, Quebec, Alberta and British Columbia, just to name the provinces with the largest number of immigrants-will be equal to, not lower

than, the amount that will be received by other pensioners in Canada who qualify for the full old age security pension or for the pension plus the guaranteed income supplement.

subsubtopic: SIXTY-FIVE YEARS OF AGE AND OVER CONTINGENT UPON RESIDENCE IN CANADA
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: SIXTY-FIVE YEARS OF AGE AND OVER CONTINGENT UPON RESIDENCE IN CANADA
speechtext:
If that was the thrust of the intervention of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre I am in full accord with him that now is the time to express this concern looking into the future and to make sure that the provinces of Ontario, Quebec, Alberta, and British Columbia will complement this legislation and provide those amounts that will be needed to protect those pensioners who immigrate to this country at an older age and have no other income. This has suddenly caught my imagination and it is an issue to which we should address ourselves at this stage in the debate.
I have listened with great interest to the interventions of other hon. members on the question of bringing the pensionable age down to 60. I must say that a number of people have spoken to me over the years of the desirability, now that we have made the first important step of reducing the pensionable age from 70 to 65, of bringing it gradually down to 60. It is mainly a concern expressed by people who work in occupations that are physically demanding. This is the case of groups such as miners, construction workers, and people who have heavy jobs in factories. They feel that by the time they are in their late fifties, they are physically worn out and they cannot continue working in jobs which they have held all their lives. Also, at that time in their lives it is extremely difficult for them to switch to another job, a so-called light job, for which there is immense demand on the labour market and a very limited supply, in order to continue to work until the magic age of 65.1 do not know whether the answer lies in providing a universal pension at the age of 65 or in providing, as the minister has indicated, a guaranteed income and a form of income supplement at whatever the pensionable age may be.
If we reduce the pensionable age to 60, we will still have to address ourselves to those who are 59, 58, and so forth. I would prefer it if we were to think in terms of coming to grips with the problem of people with limited or very low incomes, regardless of their age, through the implementation of a program that we on this side of the House have spoken about for some years, namely, the guaranteed income program plus an income supplement, because by doing so we would not limit ourselves to the pensionable age.
The minister was correct when in his previous intervention he indicated that there are people who are still vigorous and want to continue working after they reach the age of 65, and this is desirable, I suppose. Therefore we should address ourselves to meeting the needs of those who wish to retire at an earlier age because of physical conditions at work, health reasons, or the fact that after 30, 35 or even 40 years of work, if you have started working on a heavy job at the age of 15 or 16, your body cannot carry you until the age of 65 in a heavy kind of job, and it is extremely difficult, particularly if you live in rural areas, to find a light kind of job which would perhaps
March 9, 1977

permit you to carry on working until you reach the pensionable age.
It seems to me that the route indicated by the minister, which is aimed at implementing a guaranteed income and an income supplement program in the near future, is one we should all be striving to follow. I believe that members in the NDP at least have addressed themselves to this question in recent years.
Keeping in mind this principle, it was made very clear this afternoon-and I see the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) smiling-that you cannot have it both ways. You cannot ask for increased social security, increased pensions, and at the same time have someone in your party shoot you in the back by asking for a reduction in taxes. That is not what a fair and responsible government can do, and we will not have it on this side of the ITouse.

I would like to thank you, Mr. Speaker, for the opportunity to intervene in this debate. I have outlined very briefly the positive features of this bill. It seems to take a very positive approach. It introduces an element of fairness. It allows the government of Canada to enter into negotiations with countries to which Canadians migrate or from which we receive immigrants. The only concern I have is the one I expressed earlier, namely, the provision which may affect immigrants years from now if they come to Canada in their later years, if they do not join the labour force here, and particularly if they have not contributed to pension schemes in prior countries of residence.
This is something which will perhaps become clearer as the law is implemented. I certainly agree with those who spoke before me that we should make sure, either through provincial participation, under the Canada Assistance Plan or through other means, that we in Canada will not have two different standards for pensions.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to follow the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) because I want to make some comments regarding some of his arguments. He said that we in the Conservative party cannot have it both ways, that we should not be asking for tax cuts and at the same time talk about giving more to senior citizens. I could not agree with the hon. member more. That is a very reasonable thing to say, but we are not asking for it both ways, and I will demonstrate that to him at this time.
It is not a case of suggesting to the people of this country that giving money to people and taking it away from them after the death of a spouse is in some way changing the financial situation in this country. The minister told us that that cost would be $2 billion, but he failed to recognize that in his own committee he said that it may be $2 billion if we paid everybody down to the age of 60, but that it would be $700,000 if we continue to pay those on spouse's allowances. The hon. member for Davenport says we cannot have it both ways, and I agree with him.
We do not like to see things such as the Lockheed situation, the cost of the Mirabel airport, the $2 million in fees for some kinds of sales which the government cannot find, the $40 million for Argentinian nuclear plants or the $15 million lost to Eisenberg which the government cannot find, and they tell us we cannot have it both ways.

speechtext:
With regard to spouses between the ages of 60 and 65 who are married to spouses receiving the old age pension, the government says that when the older spouse dies, the money should be taken away. To say that that is equitable when the minister in committee says it is only going to cost $700,000 is a sham. That is one of the things this country should be ashamed of, and the government should be taking a stronger position on it.
We have to treat our senior citizens as human resources who have contributed and who will continue to contribute to this country. It is important that we view them as people who ought to have retirement with dignity. Canada's OAS program is interesting. We on this side feel that there is much in this bill to be commended. The old situation, which was an all or nothing situation, has been withdrawn. The new bill enables an equitable correlation between a person's contributions and his reward. There is, however, one mechanical piece of administrative detail which ought to be reviewed in terms of how this legilsation is implemented. I agree in principle that we should pay one fortieth of the total eligible pension to a person who is here one year up to a maximum of full pension to those who have been in Canada and working for 40 years. However, I do not think it is logical to suggest that a person who has been here one year should receive a cheque each month. I say this because if we take one fortieth of the present maximum pension, which is $3.55, it seems to me that it would not be economical to send out a $3.55 cheque every month.

subsubtopic: SIXTY-FIVE YEARS OF AGE AND OVER CONTINGENT UPON RESIDENCE IN CANADA
speechtext: You don't get it unless you have had ten years.

subsubtopic: SIXTY-FIVE YEARS OF AGE AND OVER CONTINGENT UPON RESIDENCE IN CANADA
speechtext:
When I was working with the Alberta government seven or eight years ago, that government would not issue a cheque for less than five dollars because it cost more than five dollars to write cheques. What the government ought to be doing is paying these pensions on an annual basis. For example, if a person has only one year's residence in Canada, instead of paying $3.55 every month, the government should simply pay a lump sum annually of $42.60. That ought to be worked out so that it does not cost extra money. I return to what the Auditor General said: let us tighten up the purse strings and manage the country a little bit better.
This bill has provisions allowing Canada to make reciprocal agreements with other countries and to share in OAS payments. I believe that is a fairly sound principle. It is particularly good in that people from other countries who come to Canada will have the advantage of a reciprocal pension agreement for those over age 65. I think, however, that those who draw up the regulations should be cautioned against writing in incentives for Canadians to work a certain period of time in this country and then move-presumably to a warmer country-where there is a reciprocal agreement and where they could draw the two pensions which would be equal to what they would receive in Canada. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) pointed out that some people will do this for health reasons, and there is justification for that. I just say that an incentive should not be built into the regula-

tions that will encourage people to move to warmer climates for their retirement years. Our senior citizens are a human resource and can continue to make a contribution to this country, so they should be enticed to remain.
While we recognize that a lot of this bill is good, Mr. Speaker, a lot has been left out. At the present time we have the concept of forced retirement in Canada, and the minister referred to this in his remarks. Labour unions, big business, and governments are all saying in effect that people are capable of working at age 64 but at age 65 they are not wanted. With modern medical technology people are living longer, as we know. I have had the honour and pleasure of travelling across this country with the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander), and we found that great numbers of senior citizens were saying that they did not want various agencies telling them that they no longer have anything to contribute, and should retire. I do not think there is any agency in this country that should determine when a person has to retire. I know the argument that older people have to be retired to make room for younger people in the work force. There is some truth in that in the area of unskilled labour and perhaps some trades, but in many areas of business the opposite is true. People with experience and knowledge in their professions or line of business are often able to generate new employment for young people, yet sometimes when they are able to give the most they are asked to retire.
The government has congratulated itself for indexing the pensions of senior citizens and for extending assistance to those who are now in the "all or nothing" situation. The fact is that at the present time the indexing relates to the consumer price index which is not necessarily consistent with the needs of senior citizens. The aged spend their money on energy, food and housing, and the indexing system in use is not correlated to these major needs. If the government had any heart at all it should look at this system. I think it is an insult to our senior citizens to receive a computerized sheet with their pension cheque telling them it is going to be increased according to the cost of living, and then find that the next month's cheque is only increased by, say, 90 cents. That does not relate or correlate to their specific needs.
The hon. member for Hamilton West mentioned the need for advertising this new bill so that senior citizens may know what it will do for them. He pointed out that the onus ought to rest with the government and not with senior citizens to find out the options open to them. I hope the minister will follow this advice.
